intro.promise: A 30-minute Friday routine will bring you warm introductions without a single event.
intro.reason_to_keep_reading: Chapter 1 shows you why the room was never the answer, and chapter 3 has you sending messages this Friday.

chapters.title: The Routine Beats the Room
chapters.goal: Replace events with a 30-minute weekly routine.
points: Why events fail introverts
What a routine gives you that a room does not
The 30-minute time box
chapters.example: Illustrative composite: an engineer turned consultant who replaced one monthly event with the Friday Five and kept the time
chapters.action_step: Block 30 minutes every Friday morning on your calendar.
chapters.transition: Next, build the list you will use.

chapters.title: Build the List of Forty
points: Where the forty names come from
Dormant ties are worth more than strangers
Cutting the list to people you would help
chapters.example: Illustrative composite: Dana sorting 400 LinkedIn connections down to 40 names in one evening
chapters.action_step: Write 40 names in a spreadsheet with one column for how you know them.

chapters.title: The Friday Five
chapters.goal: Send five short, specific messages every Friday.
points: What a Friday Five message says
Specific beats clever
Sending all five before 10 a.m.
chapters.example: Illustrative composite: Dana's first Friday Five, sent to five former colleagues, two replies within a day
chapters.action_step: Send your first Friday Five this Friday.
chapters.transition: Next, decide what each reply means.

chapters.title: Climb the Warmth Ladder
chapters.goal: Move each contact one rung at a time.
points: The four rungs: reconnect, help, ask, introduce
Signs a contact is ready for the next rung
Never skip a rung
chapters.example: Illustrative composite: a bookkeeper who moved a dormant former manager up the Warmth Ladder over six weeks
chapters.action_step: Mark each of your 40 contacts with their current rung.

chapters.title: Help First
chapters.goal: Offer something useful before any ask.
points: Small help that costs you ten minutes
Introductions you can make for others
Help that matches the contact, not you
chapters.example: Illustrative composite: Dana sending a former colleague a job lead before asking for anything
chapters.action_step: Choose one contact and send them one useful thing this week.

chapters.title: Make the Ask
points: The one-sentence ask
Who to ask for
Making it easy to say yes
chapters.example: Illustrative composite: Dana asking a former manager for an introduction to one named HR director
chapters.action_step: Write your one-sentence ask and send it to one contact on the ask rung.

chapters.title: Keep the Ask Ledger
chapters.goal: Log every ask so you learn what works.
points: The five columns of the ledger
Follow-up dates you actually keep
Reading the ledger once a month
chapters.example: Illustrative composite: a residential plumber who logged 12 asks in an Ask Ledger and learned that past customers, not other trades, sent him work
chapters.action_step: Start your Ask Ledger with every ask from the last 30 days.
chapters.transition: Next, keep the routine alive in bad weeks.

chapters.title: Protect the Routine
chapters.goal: Keep the routine running when work gets busy.
points: The minimum version for a bad week
What to do after a missed Friday
Reviewing the routine every quarter
chapters.example: Illustrative composite: the engineer turned consultant keeping the Friday Five through a three-week project crunch
chapters.action_step: Write your minimum Friday routine on the card next to your five names.

conclusion.transformation: You run a Friday routine that produces introductions on its own schedule.
conclusion.companion_course: The course gives you the message templates, the Ask Ledger sheet, and a 4-week check-in.
